scenes.title: Cold open
narration: Once banned by missionaries for its raw sexuality, this ancient Zezuru Shona mouse-and-mole dance survived by adopting the biblical name Jerusarema.
This is Mbende Jerusarema. pre-1890 to present.
on_screen: Title card: Mbende Jerusarema · Zimbabwe · pre-1890 to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originated among the Zezuru Shona people of the Murewa and Uzumba-Maramba-Pfungwe districts in Mashonaland East.
Performed across pre-colonial, colonial, and post-colonial eras, it began as an ancient fertility, military, hunting, and death ritual.
Originally named Mbende after a burrowing mouse or mole, the dance was banned by Christian missionaries in the 1910s for its perceived lewdness.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Mbende Jerusarema serves as a ritual fertility, celebration, memorial, and formerly a military diversion dance.
It symbolizes family, sexuality, rapidity, and served as a crucial source of identity and pride in the resistance against colonial power.
It is now featured at major national occasions.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed in an open space with a line of musicians continuously playing and a group of men and women taking turns dancing.
Women execute seductive, acrobatic waist-shaking and hip motions, while men crouch, jerk both arms, and vigorously kick the ground with the right leg like a burrowing mole.
Both genders culminate their movements with intense pelvic thrusts directed toward each other.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is driven by a single master drummer playing the 'mutumba' drum, which is carved from the hard wood of the mutiti or mutsvanzwa tree for acoustic resonance.
This is accompanied by men playing wooden clappers ('maja' or 'manja') made from the hard mutara tree, alongside women handclapping, yodelling, and blowing whistles and rattles.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Traditional costumes were crafted from flexible wild animal skins, including leopard, monkey, cheetah, and wild cat leather, with domestic animal skins occasionally used as inferior alternatives.
Modern dancers use a mixture of textile costumes and animal skins.
It is performed at weddings, funerals, political rallies, festivals, and recreational competitions.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Douglas Vembe, a master drummer whose efforts contributed to the dance's inscription by UNESCO.
Practiced widely across rural and urban districts of Zimbabwe, particularly centered in the Murewa and Uzumba-Maramba-Pfungwe (UPM) districts of Mashonaland East.
Maintained by the Zezuru Shona ethnic group of eastern Zimbabwe as an unbroken living ancestral tradition.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: The dance began as an ancient fertility, hunting, and death ritual with deep spiritual status for the Zezuru Shona people, though colonial suppression and modern commercialization have shifted its public contexts.
